title: Operating system and architecture check (foundational)
description: The checker reads the platform's OS name, release, and machine architecture and compares them against each tool's declared support matrix. Exact matches pass; declared-compatible families pass with a note; anything else fails fast. Checking first avoids the most frustrating failure mode: installing for an hour before discovering the binary was built for another architecture. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.
demo:
import platform
info = {'os': platform.system(), 'arch': platform.machine()}
supported = [{'os': 'Linux', 'arch': 'x86_64'}, {'os': 'Linux', 'arch': 'aarch64'}]
print('platform:', info)
print('supported:', any(s['os'] == info['os'] for s in supported))
provenance: Public computer-science methods literature (Runtime Compatibility Checker practice); cross-checked against standard references, 2026-10-21.

title: Runtime version check (foundational)
description: Required runtime versions, such as Python >= 3.9, are compared against the actual interpreter using proper version-tuple comparison, not string comparison. String comparison famously misorders versions like '3.10' versus '3.9'. The check reports the exact gap when it fails so the fix is obvious. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.
demo:
import sys
need = (3, 9)
have = sys.version_info[:2]
print('python', '.'.join(map(str, have)), '>= 3.9:', have >= need)
provenance: Public computer-science methods literature (Runtime Compatibility Checker practice); cross-checked against standard references, 2026-10-21.

title: Dependency presence check (foundational)
description: Each required package is import-checked in the current environment, recording present, missing, or wrong-version. The check runs in a subprocess when isolation matters, so a broken package cannot crash the checker itself. Results feed the compatibility report's fix list. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.

title: Hardware requirement check (foundational)
description: Hardware needs such as minimum RAM, CPU count, or GPU presence are measured against the actual machine. Measurements use standard OS interfaces rather than guesses. A tool that needs 16 GB on an 8 GB machine fails here with a clear message instead of dying mysteriously mid-run. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.
demo:
import os
cpus = os.cpu_count()
print('CPUs:', cpus, '| meets >=2 requirement:', cpus >= 2)
provenance: Public computer-science methods literature (Runtime Compatibility Checker practice); cross-checked against standard references, 2026-10-21.
